column9: stem
column14: option_a
column15: option_b
column16: option_c
column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Which of these organisms is a prokaryote?
column14: *E. coli*, a bacterium that lives in your intestines
column15: A mushroom growing on a log
column16: An amoeba from a pond
column17: An oak tree
column28: *E. coli* is a bacterium, and all bacteria are prokaryotes: cells with no nucleus. Mushrooms, oak trees and amoebas all have a nucleus, so they are eukaryotes. A common mistake is thinking any tiny single-celled thing, like an amoeba, must be a prokaryote.
column29: Prokaryotes are the cells with no nucleus. Which choice is a bacterium?

column9: Where is the DNA found in a bacterial cell?
column14: Inside a nucleus surrounded by a membrane
column15: In the nucleoid, a region of the cytoplasm with no membrane around it
column16: Inside the mitochondria
column17: In the cell wall
column28: Bacteria have one circular chromosome that sits in the nucleoid region of the cytoplasm. There is no membrane around it, because bacteria have no nucleus. Bacteria also have no mitochondria. Saying "in the nucleus" is the most common mistake.
column29: Bacteria are prokaryotes. Do they have a nucleus to hold their DNA?

column9: Bacteria and other microbes that cause disease are called ___.
column28: A pathogen is anything, such as a bacterium or virus, that causes disease. Most bacteria are not pathogens; they are helpful or harmless. Calling every bacterium a pathogen is the common mistake.
column29: The word starts with "patho-," the same root as in pathology, the study of disease.

column9: A lab report says a sample of bacteria contains cocci. What shape are these cells?
column14: Rod-shaped, like tiny hot dogs
column15: Round, like tiny spheres
column16: Square, like tiny boxes
column17: Spiral-shaped, like corkscrews
column28: Cocci (singular coccus) are round, sphere-shaped bacteria. Rods are bacilli and spirals are spirilla. Mixing up cocci and bacilli is the most common slip.
column29: Think of the round "cocoa puffs" cereal: coccus sounds like cocoa.

column9: A biologist describes a bacterium as a bacillus. Which description matches it?
column14: A long corkscrew
column15: A tiny sphere
column16: A flat, star-shaped cell
column17: A short rod, shaped a little like a pill
column28: A bacillus (plural bacilli) is rod-shaped. Spheres are cocci and corkscrews or spirals are spirilla. Bacteria don't come in star shapes in the three basic groups.
column29: There are three basic shapes: spheres, rods and spirals. Which one is a bacillus?

column9: A student draws a bacterium that is twisted like a corkscrew. Using the three basic bacteria shapes, what is this bacterium called?
column14: A nucleoid
column15: A bacillus
column16: A coccus
column17: A spirillum
column28: Spiral or corkscrew-shaped bacteria are spirilla (singular spirillum). Cocci are spheres and bacilli are rods. A nucleoid is not a shape at all; it is the region that holds a bacterium's DNA.
column29: The shape name sounds like the word "spiral."

column9: Match each part of a bacterial cell to its job.
column14: Cell wall :: Stiff outer layer that gives the cell its shape and protection
column15: Cell membrane :: Thin layer just inside the wall that controls what enters and leaves
column16: Ribosome :: Makes proteins
column17: Flagellum :: Whip-like tail that moves the cell
column18: Pili :: Short hair-like parts that help the cell stick to surfaces
column28: The cell wall gives shape and protection, the membrane controls what goes in and out, ribosomes make proteins, flagella move the cell, and pili help it stick. Students often mix up the wall and the membrane: the wall is the stiff outer layer, the membrane is just inside it.
column29: Start with the two parts that move or stick (flagellum and pili), then sort out the outer layers.

column9: Which kingdom contains the most common bacteria, the ones that live in soil, in water and on your skin?
column14: Archaebacteria
column15: Protista
column16: Fungi
column17: Eubacteria
column28: Eubacteria ("true bacteria") are the most common bacteria and live almost everywhere. Archaebacteria mostly live in extreme places. Fungi and protists are eukaryotes, not bacteria.
column29: One bacteria kingdom lives in extreme places; the other lives just about everywhere else.

column9: A single-celled prokaryote is found living in the Great Salt Lake in Utah, where the water is many times saltier than the ocean. Which kingdom does it most likely belong to?
column14: Plantae
column15: Protista
column16: Archaebacteria
column17: Eubacteria
column28: A very salty lake is an extreme environment, and extreme environments point to Archaebacteria. Eubacteria live in ordinary places. Plants and protists are eukaryotes, and this cell is a prokaryote. Picking Eubacteria just because "most bacteria are Eubacteria" is the common mistake.
column29: Is a lake that salty an ordinary place or an extreme one?

column9: The "archae-" part of the word Archaebacteria means –
column14: round
column15: true
column16: harmful
column17: ancient
column28: "Archae-" means ancient. Archaebacteria may be some of the oldest life on Earth. "Eu-" is the prefix that means true, as in Eubacteria, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Think of the word "archaeology," the study of very old things.

column9: Your textbook says bacteria are ubiquitous. What does that mean?
column14: They are found almost everywhere
column15: They are always harmful
column16: They are larger than other cells
column17: They can only live in extreme heat
column28: Ubiquitous means found everywhere. Bacteria live in soil, water, air, food and on and inside your body. It does not mean harmful; most bacteria are helpful or harmless.
column29: Think about all the places bacteria have been found: your skin, the soil, the ocean...

column9: How do bacteria reproduce?
column14: By meiosis, making eggs and sperm
column15: By releasing spores from a mushroom cap
column16: By two bacteria joining to make a seed
column17: By binary fission: one cell copies its DNA and splits into two cells
column28: Bacteria reproduce by binary fission: they copy their DNA and split in two. Meiosis and eggs and sperm belong to sexual reproduction in eukaryotes, and mushroom spores come from fungi.
column29: "Binary" means two. What happens to one bacterium when it reproduces?

column9: After a bacterium goes through binary fission, how do the two new cells compare with the original cell?
column14: They are different from each other because they had two parents
column15: One cell is alive and the other is dead
column16: Each one has half of the original cell's DNA
column17: They are genetically identical to the original cell
column28: The cell copies its whole chromosome before it splits, so each new cell gets a full, identical copy. Binary fission is asexual: there is only one parent. Thinking each cell gets half the DNA is the common mistake.
column29: The DNA is copied BEFORE the cell splits. How much DNA does each new cell get?

column9: Select every structure that a bacterial cell has. Select all that apply.
column14: Ribosomes
column15: Mitochondria
column16: Cell wall
column17: Cell membrane
column28: Bacteria have a cell wall, a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes. They are prokaryotes, so they have no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria. Choosing the nucleus is the most common mistake.
column29: Prokaryotes have no nucleus and no organelles wrapped in a membrane. Cross those out.

column9: All bacteria are harmful to humans.
column28: False. Most bacteria are helpful or harmless. Only a small number are pathogens. Bacteria help digest food, make yogurt and cheese, and recycle nutrients in the soil.
column29: Think of the bacteria in yogurt and in your gut. Are they hurting you?

column9: Bacteria in a backyard compost pile turn old leaves and food scraps into rich, dark soil. What role are these bacteria playing?
column14: Antibiotics
column15: Nitrogen fixers
column16: Decomposers
column17: Pathogens
column28: Decomposers break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil, which is exactly what happens in compost. Pathogens cause disease. Nitrogen fixers turn nitrogen gas from the air into a form plants can use; they don't break down food scraps.
column29: What do you call an organism that breaks down dead things?

column9: Plants need nitrogen, but they cannot use the nitrogen gas in the air. Which bacteria change that nitrogen gas into a form plants can use?
column14: *Lactobacillus* bacteria in yogurt
column15: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria
column16: Bacteria that break down spilled oil
column17: Disease-causing bacteria such as *Streptococcus*
column28: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria "fix" nitrogen gas into a form plants can absorb. *Streptococcus* causes strep throat, *Lactobacillus* ferments milk, and oil-eating bacteria clean up spills; none of them supply plants with nitrogen.
column29: The answer has the word "nitrogen" in its name.

column9: Which garden plant is most likely to have small bumps on its roots that are full of nitrogen-fixing bacteria?
column14: Potato plants
column15: Pea plants
column16: Tomato plants
column17: Sunflowers
column28: Peas are legumes, the plant family that includes beans, peas, clover and alfalfa. Legumes have root bumps called nodules where nitrogen-fixing bacteria live. Tomatoes, potatoes and sunflowers are not legumes.
column29: Think of the plants in the bean family.

column9: What makes cyanobacteria different from most other bacteria?
column14: They contain chlorophyll and make their own food from sunlight
column15: They are made of many cells, like animals
column16: They only live inside the human body
column17: They have a nucleus
column28: Cyanobacteria have chlorophyll and do photosynthesis, so they make their own food. They are still bacteria, so they have no nucleus. Thinking anything green must be a plant is the common mistake.
column29: Cyanobacteria are often green or blue-green. What does green pigment let an organism do?

column9: Which kingdom do cyanobacteria belong to?
column14: Archaebacteria
column15: Protista
column16: Plantae
column17: Eubacteria
column28: Cyanobacteria are true bacteria, so they are in Kingdom Eubacteria. They make their own food like plants do, but they have no nucleus, so they cannot be plants or protists. They live in ordinary ponds and lakes, not mostly in extreme places, so they are not Archaebacteria.
column29: Their name ends in "bacteria," and they live in ordinary ponds and lakes.

column9: The bacteria that always live on your skin and in your gut without making you sick are called –
column14: pathogens
column15: normal flora
column16: viruses
column17: antibiotics
column28: Normal flora are the bacteria that normally live on and in your body, and most of them help you. Pathogens cause disease, antibiotics are medicines, and viruses are not bacteria at all.
column29: These bacteria are "normal" residents of your body.

column9: A student swabs her desk and rubs the swab on a plate of agar. Two days later, small round spots appear. Each spot is a colony. What is a colony?
column14: One giant bacterium that grew big enough to see
column15: A group of viruses
column16: A drop of the agar that dried out
column17: A large group of bacteria that grew from one cell dividing over and over
column28: A colony forms when one bacterium lands on the agar and divides again and again by binary fission until there are millions of cells, enough to see. A single bacterium is far too small to see without a microscope.
column29: One bacterium is microscopic. What would it take to make a spot you can see?

column9: Select every food that is made with the help of bacteria. Select all that apply.
column14: Sour cream
column15: Bread that rises because of baker's yeast
column16: Yogurt
column17: Mushrooms on a pizza
column28: Yogurt, cheese, kimchi and sour cream are all made when bacteria ferment the sugars in milk or vegetables. Bread rises because of yeast, and mushrooms are fungi. Mixing up yeast (a fungus) with bacteria is the common mistake.
column29: Yeast and mushrooms are both in the same kingdom, and it is not a bacteria kingdom.

column9: Which bacterium is a common cause of food poisoning from undercooked chicken or eggs?
column14: Cyanobacteria
column15: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria
column16: *Salmonella*
column17: *Lactobacillus*
column28: *Salmonella* is a pathogen that can live in raw chicken and eggs and causes vomiting and diarrhea. *Lactobacillus* makes yogurt, cyanobacteria make food by photosynthesis, and nitrogen-fixing bacteria help plants. All three of those are helpful.
column29: Three of these are helpful bacteria. Which one is a pathogen?

column9: What do antibiotics do?
column14: Make helpful bacteria grow faster
column15: Kill bacteria or stop them from growing
column16: Kill viruses such as the flu
column17: Protect bacteria from your immune system
column28: Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them from growing. They do not work on viruses, which is a common misunderstanding. They don't help bacteria grow.
column29: The word "anti" means against. What are antibiotics against?

column9: Your doctor prescribes an antibiotic for 10 days. After 3 days you feel much better. What should you do?
column14: Take two pills at a time to finish faster
column15: Stop taking it and save the rest for next time
column16: Keep taking the antibiotic until all 10 days are finished
column17: Give the leftover pills to a sick friend
column28: Finish the whole prescription. Feeling better doesn't mean every bacterium is dead, and the ones that survive the first few days are often the toughest. Stopping early lets them multiply and can help antibiotic-resistant bacteria spread. Sharing or doubling doses is never safe.
column29: Feeling better and having every bacterium gone are not the same thing.

column9: Bacteria that are no longer killed by an antibiotic are called antibiotic-___ bacteria.
column28: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria survive a drug that used to kill them. Resistance belongs to the bacteria, not to the person taking the medicine, which is a common misunderstanding.
column29: The bacteria "resist" the drug.

column9: Which of these is a helpful role bacteria play in human health?
column14: Bacteria infect your throat and cause a sore throat
column15: Bacteria infect and damage your lungs
column16: Bacteria in your intestines help you digest food
column17: Bacteria in raw eggs cause vomiting
column28: Gut bacteria help break down food you couldn't digest on your own. The other three choices describe pathogens, which are harmful bacteria.
column29: Three of the choices make you sick. Which one helps you?

column9: Sauerkraut, a sour food often served with brats in Wisconsin, is made when bacteria ferment which food?
column14: Milk
column15: Ground pork
column16: Potatoes
column17: Cabbage
column28: Sauerkraut is fermented cabbage. Bacteria break down the sugars in the cabbage and make acid, which gives the sour taste and keeps the food from spoiling. Milk is what bacteria ferment to make yogurt and cheese, which is the usual mix-up.
column29: "Kraut" is the German word for cabbage.

column9: In which part of your body do most of your normal flora bacteria live?
column14: The brain
column15: The blood
column16: The large intestine
column17: The bones
column28: Trillions of bacteria live in the large intestine (your gut), where they help digest food. The brain, blood and bones are normally kept free of bacteria; bacteria in the blood are a sign of a serious infection.
column29: Think about where bacteria help with digestion.

column9: Tuberculosis (TB) is a bacterial disease that mainly attacks which organ?
column14: The lungs
column15: The stomach
column16: The eyes
column17: The skin
column28: Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium that mainly infects the lungs, causing a long-lasting cough. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs. Food poisoning is the bacterial illness that affects the stomach and intestines.
column29: TB spreads through the air when someone coughs.

column9: A single bacterium splits into 2 cells by binary fission. Then each of those 2 cells splits once. How many cells are there now?
column28: 1 cell becomes 2, and each of those 2 splits, so 2 × 2 = 4 cells. A common mistake is adding (2 + 1 = 3) instead of doubling.
column29: Each split doubles the number of cells.

column9: Which pair are the two kingdoms of bacteria?
column14: Eubacteria and Protista
column15: Eubacteria and Archaebacteria
column16: Fungi and Protista
column17: Plantae and Animalia
column28: The two bacteria kingdoms are Eubacteria (true bacteria) and Archaebacteria (ancient bacteria). Protists, fungi, plants and animals are eukaryotes with a nucleus, so none of them are bacteria.
column29: Both answers end in "bacteria."

column9: Why should chicken be cooked until it is hot all the way through?
column14: Raw chicken has no bacteria, so cooking only changes the flavor
column15: Heat kills disease-causing bacteria that may be in the raw meat
column16: Heat turns harmful bacteria into helpful bacteria
column17: Heat adds helpful bacteria to the meat
column28: Raw chicken can carry pathogens such as *Salmonella*, and cooking it to a safe temperature kills them. Cooking does not add bacteria or turn harmful ones into helpful ones. Thinking raw meat is free of bacteria is the common mistake.
column29: What does high heat do to living cells?

column9: A student finds bacteria living on a damp kitchen sponge. Which kingdom are these bacteria most likely in?
column14: Archaebacteria
column15: Plantae
column16: Fungi
column17: Eubacteria
column28: A kitchen sponge is an ordinary place, not an extreme one like a boiling hot spring, so the bacteria are most likely Eubacteria. Fungi and plants are not bacteria. Picking Archaebacteria because "bacteria" is in the name is a common slip.
column29: Is a kitchen sponge an extreme environment?

column9: Bacteria are much smaller than most plant and animal cells.
column28: True. A typical bacterium is only a few micrometers long, often 10 or more times smaller than a plant or animal cell. That is why you need a microscope at high power to see one.
column29: Bacteria have no nucleus or other organelles inside. Would you expect them to be bigger or smaller?

column9: The "eu-" in Eubacteria means –
column14: ancient
column15: true
column16: spiral
column17: extreme
column28: "Eu-" means true, so Eubacteria are the "true bacteria," the common kind found almost everywhere. "Ancient" is the meaning of "archae-" in Archaebacteria, which is the common mix-up.
column29: This is the kingdom of the common, everyday bacteria. Which meaning fits ordinary bacteria, not old or extreme ones?

column9: A yogurt label says "contains live and active cultures." What are the cultures?
column14: Living, helpful bacteria
column15: Chemicals that kill all bacteria
column16: Viruses that protect the yogurt
column17: Small pieces of fruit
column28: The "cultures" are live bacteria, such as *Lactobacillus*, that turned the milk into yogurt. They are helpful, not harmful. Thinking that any food with bacteria in it must be unsafe is the common mistake.
column29: What living things turn milk into yogurt?

column9: Green beans that are canned at home without enough heat can grow *Clostridium botulinum*, which makes a deadly poison. This is an example of bacteria –
column14: fixing nitrogen for plants
column15: being harmful by producing a toxin
column16: being helpful by fermenting food
column17: acting as normal flora
column28: *Clostridium botulinum* is a pathogen. It makes the botulism toxin, one of the strongest poisons known. Fermentation is helpful, but this bacterium is not fermenting the beans in a useful way; it is making a poison.
column29: Is a deadly poison helpful or harmful?

column9: Which bacterium is a helpful one used to make yogurt?
column14: *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*
column15: *Lactobacillus*
column16: *Salmonella*
column17: *Streptococcus pyogenes*, which causes strep throat
column28: *Lactobacillus* ferments the sugar in milk and turns it into yogurt. *Salmonella* causes food poisoning, *Streptococcus pyogenes* causes strep throat, and *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* causes TB; all three are pathogens.
column29: Its name starts with "lacto-," which has to do with milk.

column9: Bacteria have no nucleus, so they are called ___.
column28: Cells with no nucleus are prokaryotes. Cells with a nucleus, like plant and animal cells, are eukaryotes. Mixing up the two words is the common mistake.
column29: "Pro" means before and "karyon" means nucleus.

column9: Which habit best helps prevent the spread of harmful bacteria at school?
column14: Sharing water bottles with friends
column15: Washing your hands with soap and water
column16: Taking an antibiotic every day just in case
column17: Wiping your nose on your sleeve
column28: Washing with soap removes many bacteria from your hands before they can reach your mouth, nose or eyes. Sharing bottles spreads germs, and taking antibiotics when you aren't sick doesn't prevent infection and helps resistant bacteria spread.
column29: Which choice removes bacteria instead of passing them around?

column9: What would a student need in order to see individual bacteria?
column14: Just their eyes
column15: A magnifying glass
column16: A pair of binoculars
column17: A compound light microscope on high power
column28: Bacteria are only a few micrometers long, so you need a compound microscope at high power to see them. A magnifying glass only makes things a few times bigger. You can see a whole colony on agar, but not one bacterium.
column29: Bacteria are microscopic. What does that word suggest?

column9: Lyme disease, which ticks spread in Wisconsin, is caused by a –
column14: protist
column15: bacterium
column16: fungus
column17: virus
column28: Lyme disease is caused by a spiral-shaped bacterium that enters the body through the bite of an infected deer tick. Because it is a bacterium, it can be treated with antibiotics. The tick only carries the bacterium; the tick itself is not the cause.
column29: Lyme disease is treated with antibiotics. What do antibiotics work against?

column9: Every bacterium is made of just one cell. Which word describes an organism like this?
column14: Unicellular
column15: Multicellular
column16: Eukaryotic
column17: Decomposer
column28: "Uni-" means one, so a unicellular organism is made of a single cell, like every bacterium. Multicellular means many cells. Eukaryotic means having a nucleus, which bacteria don't have, and a decomposer is a role, not a cell count.
column29: Think of a unicycle: how many wheels does it have?

column9: How is a bacterial cell different from one of your cheek cells?
column14: The bacterium has mitochondria, but the cheek cell does not
column15: The cheek cell has a cell wall, but the bacterium does not
column16: The bacterium has no nucleus, and its DNA sits in the cytoplasm
column17: The bacterium has a nucleus, but the cheek cell does not
column28: A cheek cell is a eukaryotic animal cell with a nucleus and mitochondria. A bacterium is a prokaryote: no nucleus, no mitochondria, and its DNA is in the nucleoid. Animal cells have no cell wall, while bacteria do, so the choices about mitochondria, the cell wall and the nucleus all have it backwards.
column29: Which cell is the prokaryote, and what does a prokaryote lack?

column9: Why do scientists place bacteria in their own kingdoms instead of grouping them with the protists?
column14: Bacteria are many-celled, while protists are single-celled
column15: Bacteria can't reproduce, while protists can
column16: Bacteria are prokaryotes, while protists are eukaryotes with a nucleus
column17: Bacteria are bigger than protists
column28: Many bacteria and protists are both single-celled, but protists have a nucleus and other organelles, so they are eukaryotes. Bacteria have no nucleus. That basic difference in cell type separates them. Bacteria are single-celled, reproduce quickly and are smaller than protists, so the other choices are false.
column29: Both groups can be single-celled. What is different inside the cells?

column9: Select every place where you would most likely find Archaebacteria. Select all that apply.
column14: A kitchen counter
column15: A boiling hot spring in Yellowstone
column16: A cup of yogurt
column17: A person's infected throat
column18: A lake that is far saltier than the ocean
column19: A hot vent on the deep ocean floor
column28: Archaebacteria are best known for living in extreme places: boiling hot springs, very salty lakes and deep-sea vents. Yogurt, a kitchen counter and an infected throat are ordinary places where Eubacteria live. Thinking all bacteria live in the same kinds of places is the common mistake.
column29: Look for the places that would kill most other living things.

column9: The prefix "staphylo-" means a bunch of grapes. What would *Staphylococcus* bacteria look like under a microscope?
column14: Rod-shaped cells grouped in clusters
column15: Round cells lined up in a single chain
column16: Round cells grouped in grape-like clusters
column17: Spiral cells lined up end to end
column28: Break the name apart: "staphylo-" means grape-like clusters and "-coccus" means round. So *Staphylococcus* is clusters of round cells. Round cells in chains would be *Streptococcus*, and rods would be bacilli.
column29: Split the name into two parts: one tells the arrangement, one tells the shape.

column9: "Strepto-" means in chains and "diplo-" means in pairs. Under a microscope, a student sees rod-shaped cells lined up end to end in long chains. Which name fits these bacteria?
column14: Streptobacilli
column15: Spirilla
column16: Streptococci
column17: Diplococci
column28: Rods are bacilli and chains are "strepto-," so chains of rods are streptobacilli. Streptococci are chains of round cells, diplococci are round cells in pairs, and spirilla are spirals. Choosing streptococci by matching only the "chain" part is the common mistake.
column29: Combine the arrangement prefix with the shape word.

column9: Why can a few bacteria left on a kitchen counter become millions of bacteria in less than a day?
column14: Each bacterium grows into a many-celled organism
column15: Each bacterium can split in two in as little as 20 minutes, so the number keeps doubling
column16: Bacteria are made from the dust on the counter
column17: Bacteria pair up and lay hundreds of eggs
column28: Under good conditions some bacteria divide by binary fission every 20 minutes. Each division doubles the population, so the numbers grow very fast. Bacteria don't lay eggs, don't form from dust, and stay single-celled.
column29: What happens to the total number each time every cell splits once?

column9: Put the steps of binary fission in order.
column14: The cell grows longer and the two DNA copies move toward opposite ends
column15: The cell splits into two identical daughter cells
column16: The cell makes a copy of its single circular chromosome
column17: The cell membrane and cell wall pinch inward across the middle of the cell
column28: Copy the DNA → grow and pull the copies apart → pinch in the middle → split into two identical cells. A common mistake is putting the split before the DNA is copied, which would leave one cell with no DNA.
column29: The DNA has to be copied and moved apart before the cell can split.

column9: A Wisconsin dairy farmer grows alfalfa in a field for three years, then plants corn there. The corn needs much less nitrogen fertilizer than corn planted after corn. Why?
column14: Corn roots make their own nitrogen after alfalfa is removed
column15: Bacteria living in the alfalfa's roots added usable nitrogen to the soil
column16: Alfalfa roots are pathogens that kill the weeds that steal nitrogen
column17: Alfalfa releases oxygen that turns into nitrogen in the soil
column28: Alfalfa is a legume. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in its root nodules turn nitrogen gas into a form plants can use, and some of it stays in the soil for the next crop. Corn cannot fix nitrogen, and oxygen does not turn into nitrogen.
column29: Alfalfa is in the same plant family as beans and peas.

column9: Scientists think ancient cyanobacteria changed Earth's atmosphere billions of years ago. How did they change it?
column14: They used up the oxygen by causing disease
column15: They removed all the nitrogen gas from the air
column16: They released oxygen gas through photosynthesis
column17: They released carbon dioxide by decomposing rocks
column28: Early Earth had almost no oxygen gas. Cyanobacteria did photosynthesis for millions of years and gave off oxygen, which built up in the air. Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and releases oxygen, so the carbon dioxide choice has it backwards.
column29: What gas does photosynthesis give off?

column9: Imagine that every decomposer bacterium in a Wisconsin forest suddenly disappeared. What would most likely happen over the next several years?
column14: Nothing would change, because decomposers do not affect plants
column15: Animals would stop dying, because there would be no bacteria
column16: Dead leaves and animals would pile up, and the soil would run low on nutrients for new plants
column17: Trees would grow faster because no bacteria would compete with them
column28: Decomposers break down dead material and return its nutrients to the soil. Without them, dead things would build up and the nutrients would stay locked inside them, so new plants would struggle. Decomposers are not mainly disease-causers, so removing them would not stop animals from dying.
column29: Where do the nutrients in a dead leaf go after it rots?

column9: How do the normal flora bacteria on your skin and in your gut help protect you from pathogens?
column14: They make vaccines inside your body
column15: They take up space and food, so harmful bacteria have a harder time growing
column16: They kill every virus that enters your body
column17: They turn into white blood cells
column28: Normal flora crowd the surfaces of your skin and gut and use up the food there, so a pathogen that arrives has less room and food to grow. They don't become white blood cells, make vaccines or kill viruses.
column29: Think of a parking lot that is already full. What happens when a new car shows up?

column9: As bacteria turn milk into yogurt, they produce acid. What happens to the pH of the milk?
column14: The pH goes down, because the milk becomes more acidic
column15: The pH goes up, because the milk becomes more basic
column16: The pH stays the same, because bacteria do not change pH
column17: The pH goes up, because the milk becomes more acidic
column28: Acids have a pH below 7, and adding acid lowers the pH. Milk starts at about 6.5 and yogurt ends up around 4.5. Thinking that more acid means a higher pH is the common mistake: on the pH scale, lower numbers are more acidic.
column29: On the pH scale, are acids the low numbers or the high numbers?

column9: Select every illness that is caused by bacteria. Select all that apply.
column14: The common cold
column15: Influenza (the flu)
column16: Whooping cough
column17: Chickenpox
column28: Whooping cough, tuberculosis and tetanus are bacterial diseases, so antibiotics can treat them. The common cold, the flu and chickenpox are caused by viruses, and antibiotics do not work on them. Thinking every illness is caused by bacteria is the common mistake.
column29: Three of these are caused by viruses. Which ones would a flu shot or chickenpox vaccine target?

column9: Which example shows bacteria helping the ENVIRONMENT, rather than helping human health directly?
column14: Soil bacteria breaking down a dead raccoon
column15: Engineered bacteria making insulin for people with diabetes
column16: *Lactobacillus* turning milk into yogurt
column17: Gut bacteria helping you digest food
column28: Breaking down a dead animal recycles nutrients back into the soil, which helps the ecosystem. Digestion, yogurt and insulin all help people directly. Choosing yogurt because it is "natural" is a common slip.
column29: Which choice would still matter even if no people were around?

column9: Select every example of bacteria being HARMFUL to people. Select all that apply.
column14: Bacteria infecting and damaging lung tissue
column15: Bacteria breaking down oil spilled on a beach
column16: Bacteria turning cabbage into sauerkraut
column17: Bacteria in undercooked eggs causing vomiting and diarrhea
column18: Gut bacteria helping you digest food
column19: Bacteria on teeth releasing acid that causes cavities
column28: Food poisoning, tooth decay and lung infections are harmful. Cleaning up oil, making sauerkraut and helping digestion are helpful roles. A common mistake is calling tooth decay "not bacteria"; cavities are caused by acid that mouth bacteria make from sugar.
column29: For each choice, ask: does this make a person sick or damage the body?

column9: Under ideal conditions, a certain bacterium divides by binary fission every 20 minutes. Starting with 1 bacterium, how many bacteria will there be after 1 hour?
column28: 1 hour = 60 minutes = 3 divisions of 20 minutes. The number doubles each time: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8. A common mistake is multiplying 1 × 3 = 3 instead of doubling three times.
column29: First figure out how many 20-minute periods fit in an hour. Then double that many times.

column9: Put the steps for making yogurt at home in order.
column14: The milk thickens and turns sour as acid builds up
column15: Keep the milk warm for several hours while the bacteria ferment the milk sugar
column16: Stir in a spoonful of yogurt that contains live cultures
column17: Heat the milk to kill unwanted bacteria
column18: Let the milk cool until it is warm, not hot
column28: Heat → cool → add live bacteria → keep warm while they ferment → the milk thickens and sours. A common mistake is adding the live cultures before the milk cools, but hot milk would kill the helpful bacteria too.
column29: What would happen to the helpful bacteria if you added them to very hot milk?

column9: Beef jerky is dried and salted, and it can sit on a shelf for months without spoiling. Why does drying and salting keep bacteria from spoiling it?
column14: Drying adds helpful bacteria that make the jerky taste better
column15: Salt turns bacteria into viruses
column16: Bacteria need water to grow, and drying and salting remove the water they could use
column17: Bacteria only grow in cold places
column28: Like all living cells, bacteria need water. Drying removes water, and salt pulls water out of bacterial cells. Bacteria actually grow faster when it is warm, not cold, which is why we refrigerate many foods.
column29: What do all living cells need that dry, salty jerky doesn't have much of?

column9: A student grows bacteria on two agar plates. Plate A is kept at 37 °C (body temperature) and Plate B is kept in a refrigerator at 4 °C. After 2 days, Plate A has many colonies and Plate B has very few. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: Bacteria need light to grow
column15: 37 °C is too hot for bacteria to grow
column16: Cold temperatures slow down bacterial growth
column17: Cold temperatures kill all bacteria
column28: Plate B still has a few colonies, so cold did not kill all the bacteria; it slowed their growth. The plates differed in temperature, not light. Plate A grew the most, so 37 °C was not too hot. Saying the refrigerator "kills" bacteria is the common mistake.
column29: Plate B has very few colonies, not zero. What does that tell you?

column9: Which statement correctly compares a bacterium with a virus?
column14: A virus is a living cell, but a bacterium is not
column15: Bacteria and viruses are the same thing with different names
column16: A virus is bigger than a bacterium and has a nucleus
column17: A bacterium is a living cell with ribosomes that can reproduce on its own; a virus is not a cell
column28: Bacteria are living prokaryotic cells with a cell wall and ribosomes, and they reproduce by binary fission. Viruses are not cells; they can only make copies of themselves inside a host cell. That is why antibiotics, which attack bacterial parts, have nothing to target in a virus. Viruses are also much smaller than bacteria.
column29: Which one reproduces by binary fission?

column9: A lab places a paper disk soaked in the antibiotic ampicillin on a plate covered with bacteria. After two days, the bacteria have grown right up to the edge of the disk. What is the best explanation?
column14: Ampicillin kills these bacteria very well
column15: These bacteria are resistant to ampicillin
column16: These bacteria are viruses, so the antibiotic could not reach them
column17: Ampicillin is a food that all bacteria need
column28: If an antibiotic works, it leaves a clear ring with no growth around the disk. Bacteria growing right up to the disk means the drug did not stop them, so they are resistant. Antibiotics are not food, and bacteria are not viruses.
column29: If the drug killed the bacteria, what would you see around the disk?

column9: Why do scientists who study how life on early Earth might have looked often study Archaebacteria?
column14: Archaebacteria survive in extreme conditions like those on early Earth and may be some of the oldest life
column15: Archaebacteria have a nucleus like the first animals
column16: Archaebacteria are the most complex organisms alive
column17: Archaebacteria are the newest kind of life on Earth
column28: Early Earth was hot and harsh. Archaebacteria thrive in very hot, salty or otherwise extreme places, and their name means "ancient bacteria." They are simple prokaryotes with no nucleus, not complex or new.
column29: What does the "archae-" in their name mean?

column9: *Streptococcus mutans* bacteria in your mouth feed on sugar and give off acid that eats away tooth enamel. Which habit would do the most to prevent cavities?
column14: Brushing your teeth and eating fewer sugary snacks
column15: Brushing only once a week but using more toothpaste
column16: Rinsing with sugary sports drinks
column17: Taking antibiotics every day
column28: Brushing removes the bacteria, and less sugar means less food for them to turn into acid. Daily antibiotics would harm helpful bacteria and help resistant bacteria spread. Sugary drinks feed the bacteria.
column29: The bacteria need sugar to make acid. How could you take away their food and remove them?

column9: Bacteria such as *Lactobacillus* turn the sugar in milk into ___ acid, which makes yogurt taste sour.
column28: *Lactobacillus* bacteria ferment lactose (milk sugar) into lactic acid. The acid gives yogurt its sour taste and makes the milk thicken. "Lactose" is the sugar, not the acid, which is the common mix-up.
column29: The acid's name comes from the Latin word for milk, the same root as in *Lactobacillus*.

column9: Cows can't digest the tough cellulose in grass by themselves. Bacteria living in the cow's stomach break the cellulose down. How would you describe this relationship?
column14: Harmful: the bacteria are pathogens that make the cow sick
column15: The bacteria are fixing nitrogen for the grass
column16: Helpful: the bacteria get food and a home, and the cow gets nutrients from grass
column17: The bacteria are decomposers breaking down the dead cow
column28: The bacteria get food and a warm place to live, and the cow gets nutrients it couldn't get on its own, so both benefit. This works the same way as your own gut bacteria helping you digest food. The cow is alive, so the bacteria are not decomposing it.
column29: Who gets something out of this deal: the bacteria, the cow, or both?

column9: Match each problem to the way bacteria can help solve it.
column14: Oil spilled on a beach :: Add bacteria that break down the oil
column15: A person with diabetes needs insulin :: Use bacteria engineered with the human insulin gene to make it
column16: A town's sewage must be cleaned :: Bacteria in treatment tanks break down the waste
column17: Dead leaves pile up in the fall :: Soil bacteria break them down and return nutrients to the soil
column28: Oil-eating bacteria clean up spills, engineered bacteria make human insulin, wastewater bacteria break down sewage, and decomposer bacteria recycle dead leaves into soil nutrients. Thinking bacteria are only germs hides all of these helpful jobs.
column29: Match the oil and insulin first; they are the most specific.

column9: A type of *E. coli* lives harmlessly in a cow's intestines. If it gets into undercooked hamburger, a person who eats the burger can get very sick. What does this show?
column14: All *E. coli* are always dangerous to every animal
column15: The same kind of bacteria can be harmless in one place and harmful in another
column16: Cooking meat makes bacteria stronger
column17: *E. coli* is a virus, not a bacterium
column28: This strain doesn't hurt the cow but makes people sick, and most *E. coli* in your own gut are helpful normal flora. Whether bacteria help or harm depends on the kind and the place. Cooking kills bacteria; it doesn't strengthen them.
column29: Does the cow get sick? Does the person?

column9: Which observation would best show that a mystery cell is a bacterium and not a plant cell?
column14: It is green
column15: It has no nucleus
column16: It has a cell wall
column17: It has ribosomes
column28: Plant cells have a nucleus, and bacteria never do, so no nucleus points to a bacterium. Plant cells also have cell walls and ribosomes, so those don't tell the two apart. Some bacteria, like cyanobacteria, are green too.
column29: Cross out every feature that BOTH bacteria and plant cells can have.

column9: Your little brother has a fever and a sore throat. Which test result would mean an antibiotic could help him?
column14: A test shows he has seasonal allergies
column15: A nose swab tests positive for the flu virus
column16: A test shows he has a cold virus
column17: A throat swab tests positive for *Streptococcus* bacteria
column28: Antibiotics kill bacteria, so they help only when the illness is bacterial, like strep throat. The flu and colds are viruses, and allergies are not infections at all. Asking for antibiotics for every sore throat is the common mistake.
column29: Which result names a bacterium?

column9: Which statement correctly compares Archaebacteria and Eubacteria?
column14: Eubacteria live only in extreme environments
column15: Archaebacteria have a nucleus, but Eubacteria do not
column16: Both are prokaryotes, but Archaebacteria usually live in extreme environments
column17: Archaebacteria are many-celled, but Eubacteria are single-celled
column28: Both kingdoms are single-celled prokaryotes with no nucleus. The big difference you need is where they live: Archaebacteria in extreme places, Eubacteria almost everywhere else. Swapping the two habitats is the common mistake.
column29: Do either of these kingdoms have a nucleus?

column9: Penicillin kills bacteria by damaging the cell wall they are building. Why doesn't penicillin damage your own body's cells?
column14: Penicillin only works outside the body
column15: Human cells have thicker cell walls than bacteria
column16: Human cells have a nucleus that blocks penicillin
column17: Human cells have no cell wall, so penicillin has nothing to attack
column28: Animal cells, including yours, have a cell membrane but no cell wall. Penicillin targets a structure bacteria have and you don't. The nucleus has nothing to do with it, and saying human cells have thicker walls is the common mistake; they have no wall at all.
column29: Think about which cell parts bacteria have that animal cells lack.

column9: After a long course of a strong antibiotic, some people get an upset stomach and diarrhea. What is the most likely reason?
column14: The antibiotic made the person's cells grow cell walls
column15: The antibiotic turned into a virus in the stomach
column16: The antibiotic added extra bacteria to the gut
column17: The antibiotic also killed many of the helpful bacteria in the gut that aid digestion
column28: Antibiotics cannot tell pathogens apart from helpful normal flora, so a strong one kills many gut bacteria too. With fewer helpful bacteria, digestion is upset and harmful bacteria can take over the empty space. Antibiotics don't become viruses or add bacteria.
column29: Does an antibiotic know which bacteria are the "bad" ones?

column9: In late summer, some Wisconsin lakes turn bright green from "blue-green algae," which are actually cyanobacteria, a type of bacteria. Dogs that swim in the water can get sick from toxins they make. What does this show about cyanobacteria?
column14: Cyanobacteria are Archaebacteria because they live in lakes
column15: Cyanobacteria are algae, so they are plants
column16: The same group can be helpful, by making oxygen, and harmful, by making toxins
column17: Cyanobacteria are always harmful and never make oxygen
column28: Cyanobacteria do photosynthesis and release oxygen, which is helpful, but large blooms can make toxins that harm animals. They are bacteria (Eubacteria), not plants or algae, despite the nickname. A lake is not an extreme environment, so they are not Archaebacteria.
column29: Remember what cyanobacteria give off when they make food, then think about what the toxins do.

column9: At a picnic, one bacterium lands on a potato salad at 12:00 noon. In the warm sun, the bacteria double every 30 minutes. How many bacteria will be on the salad at 3:00 PM?
column28: Noon to 3:00 PM is 3 hours = 180 minutes = 6 divisions of 30 minutes. Doubling 6 times: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32 → 64. A common mistake is doubling once per hour (only 3 times, giving 8).
column29: Count the 30-minute periods between noon and 3:00 PM first.

column9: A culture starts with 50 bacteria, and the population doubles every hour. How many bacteria will there be after 4 hours?
column28: Doubling 4 times multiplies by 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16, so 50 × 16 = 800. A common mistake is multiplying by 4 × 2 = 8 instead of doubling four separate times, which gives 400.
column29: Double 50, then double that answer, and keep going until you have doubled 4 times.

column9: Starting with a single bacterium, how many rounds of binary fission does it take to produce 1,024 cells?
column28: Each round doubles the number: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1,024. That is 10 rounds (2¹⁰ = 1,024). A common mistake is counting the starting cell as a round, or stopping at 512.
column29: Keep doubling from 1 and count how many times you double until you reach 1,024.

column9: An infection contains 2,000,000 bacteria. An antibiotic kills 99% of them in the first two days. How many bacteria survive?
column28: If 99% are killed, 1% survive: 0.01 × 2,000,000 = 20,000. These survivors are often the toughest, which is why stopping an antibiotic early can let resistant bacteria take over. A common mistake is calculating the number killed (1,980,000) instead of the number that survive.
column29: What percent of the bacteria are NOT killed?

column9: Milk has a pH of about 6.5. After bacteria ferment it into yogurt, the pH is about 4.5. Each drop of 1 on the pH scale means 10 times more acidic. How many times more acidic is the yogurt than the milk?
column28: The pH dropped by 2 units, and each unit is a factor of 10, so the yogurt is 10 × 10 = 100 times more acidic. A common mistake is answering 2 (just the difference) or 20 (multiplying 2 × 10).
column29: Find how many pH units it dropped, then multiply by 10 once for each unit.

column9: Put the steps in order to show how antibiotic-resistant bacteria become common in an infection.
column14: The person takes the antibiotic
column15: The antibiotic kills most of the bacteria that are not resistant
column16: An infection contains many bacteria, and a few of them happen to have a gene that resists the antibiotic
column17: Most of the bacteria in the infection are now resistant to the antibiotic
column18: The resistant bacteria that survive reproduce by binary fission
column28: The resistant bacteria are already there before the drug is taken; the antibiotic kills the others, and the survivors multiply until they make up most of the population. A common mistake is thinking the antibiotic causes bacteria to become resistant. It only selects the ones that already were.
column29: Were the resistant bacteria there before or after the person took the medicine?

column9: Put these steps in order to show how nitrogen gets from the air into a rabbit and back to the soil.
column14: The rabbit dies, and decomposer bacteria return its nitrogen to the soil
column15: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the roots of a clover plant change the nitrogen into a form plants can use
column16: The clover uses the nitrogen to build proteins
column17: A rabbit eats the clover
column18: Nitrogen gas (N₂) makes up most of the air, but plants can't use it
column28: Air → nitrogen-fixing bacteria → plant proteins → animal that eats the plant → decomposers return nitrogen to the soil. Bacteria are needed at both ends of the cycle. A common mistake is thinking plants pull nitrogen gas straight from the air.
column29: The plant can't use nitrogen until the bacteria change it.

column9: A student says, "Since bacteria cause diseases, the world would be better off if we killed every bacterium." Which response best evaluates this claim?
column14: The claim is right, because bacteria have no role in ecosystems
column15: The claim is right, because all bacteria are pathogens
column16: The claim is wrong: without bacteria, dead things would not decompose, plants would lack usable nitrogen, and our digestion would suffer
column17: The claim is wrong only because killing bacteria would be too expensive
column28: Most bacteria are helpful or harmless. They decompose dead material, fix nitrogen for plants, make oxygen, and help us digest food. Losing all of them would collapse ecosystems and harm our health. The claim's mistake is treating a few pathogens as if they were all bacteria.
column29: List the helpful jobs bacteria do. What would happen to each one?

column9: Newborn babies are given a vitamin K shot right after birth. Using what you know about normal flora, which explanation makes the most sense?
column14: Vitamin K kills the pathogens a baby picks up at birth
column15: Babies' cells don't have ribosomes, so they need extra vitamins
column16: Newborns have too many gut bacteria, which destroy vitamin K
column17: A newborn's intestines do not yet have the bacteria that make vitamin K
column28: Gut bacteria such as *E. coli* make vitamin K, which helps blood clot. A newborn's intestines start out with very few bacteria, so the baby can't get enough vitamin K from them yet. Vitamin K is not an antibiotic, and every human cell has ribosomes.
column29: Where do adults get some of their vitamin K? Does a newborn have that yet?

column9: Cyanobacteria carry out photosynthesis, but they have no chloroplasts. How is that possible?
column14: Their chlorophyll sits on folded membranes in the cytoplasm, because prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles
column15: Their nucleus does photosynthesis instead
column16: They borrow chloroplasts from nearby plant cells
column17: They don't really do photosynthesis; they eat plants
column28: Chloroplasts are membrane-bound organelles, which prokaryotes lack. Cyanobacteria still have chlorophyll, held on membranes inside the cytoplasm, so they can do photosynthesis without chloroplasts. They have no nucleus either, so that choice is impossible.
column29: Think about what kind of cell parts every prokaryote is missing.

column9: A student spreads bacteria over an agar plate and places three paper disks soaked in different antibiotics on it. After two days, Antibiotic X has a clear ring 22 mm wide around it, Antibiotic Y has a clear ring 8 mm wide, and Antibiotic Z has no clear ring. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: Antibiotic Z was the most effective because no bacteria grew on it
column15: All three antibiotics worked equally well
column16: Antibiotic X was the most effective against these bacteria, and the bacteria are resistant to Z
column17: The bacteria are resistant to X because the ring is the largest
column28: The clear ring is where bacteria could not grow, so a wider ring means the antibiotic stopped more bacteria. X has the widest ring and Z has none, which means Z did not stop them. Reading "no ring" as "best" is the common mistake.
column29: What does a clear ring around a disk tell you happened there?

column9: A cell is collected from water near a vent on the deep ocean floor, where the temperature is above 100 °C. It is rod-shaped, has a cell wall and has no nucleus. Which description fits it best?
column14: A bacillus in Kingdom Archaebacteria
column15: A rod-shaped protist
column16: A coccus in Kingdom Eubacteria
column17: A spirillum in Kingdom Archaebacteria
column28: No nucleus means it is a prokaryote, so it is not a protist. The extreme heat of a deep-sea vent points to Archaebacteria. A rod shape is a bacillus. The other choices get either the shape or the kingdom wrong.
column29: Decide three things in order: nucleus or not, extreme home or ordinary, and shape.

column9: Which change would most likely make antibiotic-resistant bacteria MORE common in a community?
column14: Doctors testing for bacteria before prescribing antibiotics
column15: People washing their hands more often
column16: Patients finishing every antibiotic prescription
column17: Doctors prescribing antibiotics for colds and the flu
column28: Colds and flu are caused by viruses, so antibiotics do nothing for them but still kill many of the person's non-resistant bacteria. That leaves resistant bacteria with less competition to multiply and spread. The other three choices all lower resistance.
column29: Three of these choices reduce how often antibiotics are used without a reason. Which one increases it?

column9: Select every structure found in a bacterial cell that is ALSO found in a human cheek cell. Select all that apply.
column14: Ribosomes
column15: Cell wall
column16: Cell membrane
column17: Pili
column18: A single circular chromosome in a nucleoid
column28: Both cells have a cell membrane, ribosomes and cytoplasm. Animal cells have no cell wall, keep their DNA in a nucleus rather than a nucleoid, and don't have pili. Choosing the cell wall is the most common mistake.
column29: Picture an animal cell. Does it have a stiff wall? Where does it keep its DNA?

column9: Students grow bacteria from four swabs on agar plates and count the colonies after two days: doorknob, 85; phone screen, 120; unwashed hand, 95; hand right after washing with soap, 6. Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
column14: Every bacterium on the phone screen causes disease
column15: Washing with soap kills 100% of bacteria
column16: Washing with soap greatly reduced the number of bacteria on the hand
column17: Doorknobs carry more bacteria than anything else tested
column28: The washed hand dropped from 95 to 6 colonies, a big reduction, but not to zero, so soap did not remove 100%. The data count bacteria; they don't show whether any are pathogens. The phone (120), not the doorknob, had the most.
column29: Compare the two hand plates. Did the washed hand reach zero?

column9: Bean plants grow well in a farmer's field without any nitrogen fertilizer. When the same kind of beans are grown in soil that was heated to kill every bacterium in it, the plants turn yellow and grow poorly. What is the best explanation?
column14: The bacteria in the field were pathogens that the beans needed to fight
column15: Without nitrogen-fixing bacteria, the beans could not get enough usable nitrogen
column16: Heating the soil added too much nitrogen
column17: Beans can only grow in the dark
column28: Beans rely on nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root nodules for usable nitrogen. Killing the bacteria removed that supply, so the plants were starved of nitrogen and turned yellow. Heating soil does not add nitrogen, and the field bacteria were helpful, not pathogens.
column29: What did the heated soil lose that the field soil still had?

column9: A student says, "I've taken antibiotics so many times that my body has become resistant to them." Which correction is best?
column14: The student is right; bodies build up resistance to antibiotics the way they do to vaccines
column15: Resistance is impossible, because antibiotics always kill every bacterium
column16: The student is right; antibiotics turn into viruses after many uses
column17: Bodies don't become resistant; bacteria do, because the resistant ones survive the drug and multiply
column28: Antibiotic resistance is a property of bacteria. Each time an antibiotic is used, the bacteria that already resist it survive and reproduce, so resistant bacteria become more common. The person's body has not changed. Confusing resistance with immunity from vaccines is the common mistake.
column29: Which living things does the antibiotic act on: your cells or the bacteria?

column9: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. How many minutes will it take for 1 bacterium to become 16 bacteria?
column28: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 takes 4 doublings, and 4 × 20 minutes = 80 minutes. A common mistake is dividing 16 by 2 to get 8 doublings (160 minutes).
column29: Count the doublings from 1 to 16, then multiply by the time for each one.

column9: A prokaryote is found in an acidic hot spring with a pH of 2 and a temperature of 80 °C. A classmate says it must be in Kingdom Eubacteria, because "all prokaryotes are Eubacteria." Which response is best?
column14: The classmate is right: Archaebacteria have a nucleus, so they can't be prokaryotes
column15: The classmate is wrong: it must be a protist, because protists live in hot springs
column16: The classmate is wrong: both bacteria kingdoms are prokaryotes, and the extreme hot, acidic home points to Archaebacteria
column17: The classmate is right: only Eubacteria are prokaryotes
column28: Eubacteria and Archaebacteria are both prokaryotes, so "no nucleus" alone can't decide between them. The hot, very acidic spring is an extreme environment, which points to Archaebacteria. Protists have a nucleus, so this prokaryote can't be one, and Archaebacteria have no nucleus.
column29: Being a prokaryote narrows it to two kingdoms. What clue picks between them?

column9: Which experiment would best test whether a new hand soap removes more bacteria than washing with plain water?
column14: Have everyone wash with the new soap, then swab their hands and count colonies
column15: Have one person wash with soap and another with water, using different agar and different temperatures
column16: Ask students whether their hands feel cleaner after using the soap
column17: Swab everyone's hands, have half wash with the soap and half with plain water for the same time, swab again, then grow all swabs at the same temperature and compare colony counts
column28: A fair test needs a control group (plain water), the same washing time, the same growing conditions, and a measurement (colony counts) before and after. Using only soap has no comparison, changing several variables at once makes the result unclear, and "feeling cleaner" isn't a measurement of bacteria.
column29: A good experiment changes only one thing and has something to compare against.

column9: Bacteria in a flask of broth divide every 20 minutes at first, but after many hours the population stops growing even though the flask is still warm. What is the most likely reason?
column14: Each bacterium can only divide 10 times in its life
column15: The bacteria have used up the food and built up waste, so they can no longer keep dividing
column16: The flask became too cold for the bacteria
column17: The bacteria turned into viruses
column28: Bacteria need food, water and space. In a closed flask, they eventually use up the nutrients and their own wastes build up, so growth stops. The stem says the flask is still warm, so cold isn't the reason, and bacteria don't turn into viruses.
column29: A closed flask has a limited amount of something bacteria need. What runs out?

column9: In which relationship do BOTH the bacteria and the other organism benefit?
column14: *Streptococcus pyogenes* living in a person's throat
column15: *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* living in a person's lungs
column16: Normal flora bacteria living in a person's large intestine
column17: *Salmonella* living in a person's intestines
column28: Normal flora get food and a home, and in return they help digest food, make vitamins and crowd out pathogens. *Salmonella*, *Streptococcus pyogenes* and *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* benefit while the person gets sick, so only the bacteria gain. The common mistake is thinking any bacteria living inside you must be harmful.
column29: In three of the choices, the person gets sick. Which one helps the person?
